*All rates listed in this article are based on average mortgage rate data. A real borrower's rates and APRs will vary from these averages based on their credit score, income, debt, down payment size, home type, and location.*

Keep in mind every lender prices loans differently based on credit score, down payment, loan size, and property type, so the rate you're quoted will not match the national average exactly.


## What's moving rates this week


After climbing for most of the past month, rates finally caught a break on Thursday. The average 30-year fixed fell 0.06% to 7.54%, one of the few meaningful daily declines in recent weeks. Government-backed loans saw the biggest improvement: FHA rates dropped 0.10% to 7.15%, and VA rates fell 0.08% to 7.17%.


Thursday's dip followed a rough midweek stretch. On Wednesday, rates started the day on a promising note after a lower inflation reading, but bond markets weakened as the session went on and the 30-year fixed closed at 7.60%, its highest daily average in nearly three years.


No single headline explains Thursday's turnaround. Several factors likely contributed: investors adjusting positions ahead of Friday's jobs report, concerns about government bond markets in parts of Europe, reassuring comments from Fed officials that helped ease expectations for further rate hikes, and buying interest after the 10-year Treasury yield reached a multi-year high.


Not every product moved lower. The 30-year jumbo held at 7.66% and the 7/6 SOFR ARM edged up 0.02% to 6.87%, with both sitting at the top of their 52-week ranges. Over the past year, every major product is up more than a full percentage point, led by the jumbo (+1.39 points) and the 15-year fixed (+1.30 points).


This morning's jobs report showed the economy added far fewer jobs in September than forecasts expected, and the unemployment rate ticked up slightly, to about 4.2%. Weaker job growth often helps rates, and mortgage bonds rallied early in the session. Much of that improvement had faded by midday, though, in part because unemployment stayed relatively stable, which makes the report look less weak than the headline job count suggests.

## Fixed vs. ARM vs. government-backed: which rate fits you?


Not every borrower is shopping for the same loan, and the "best" rate depends on which product fits your situation:


- **30-year fixed** offers predictable payments for the life of the loan. It's the most common choice for buyers who plan to stay in the home long-term or simply want payment stability. See[fixed vs. adjustable-rate mortgages](https://better.com/content/fixed-vs-adjustable-rate-mortgage) for a full breakdown of how the two compare.
- **7/6 SOFR ARM** starts with a lower initial rate — currently averaging 6.87%, 0.67 points below today's 7.54% 30-year fixed rate — that adjusts every six months after an initial seven-year fixed period. Our[7/6 ARM guide](https://better.com/content/7-6-arm) explains how the rate resets work, and this can make sense for borrowers who expect to sell, refinance, or pay off the loan before the adjustable period begins — though it carries the risk that rates could be higher when it resets. Our guide on[refinancing an ARM loan](https://better.com/content/can-you-refinance-an-arm-loan) covers your options before that reset window arrives.
- **FHA loans** (7.15%) allow for lower down payments and more flexible credit requirements, backed by the Federal Housing Administration, but require mortgage insurance premiums that don't automatically go away like conventional PMI in most cases. See[FHA vs. conventional loans](https://better.com/content/fha-vs-conventional-loans) for a fuller comparison.
- **VA loans** (7.17%) are available to eligible veterans, active-duty service members, and some surviving spouses, often with no down payment required and no ongoing mortgage insurance. Our[VA loan vs. FHA](https://better.com/content/va-loan-vs-fha) breakdown covers which program tends to cost less depending on your situation.
- **Jumbo loans** (7.66%) apply to loan amounts above the conforming loan limit set by the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) each year, and typically carry stricter credit and reserve requirements. Our[jumbo vs. conventional loan](https://better.com/content/jumbo-vs-conventional-loan) guide walks through when a jumbo loan is the right call.


Not sure what kind of loan you need? A pre-approval can estimate payments for different loans — you can[get pre-approved](https://better.com/preapproval) in as little as a few minutes.


## Should you lock today or wait?


There's no universal answer to this question, and buyers should be wary of anyone who guarantees predictions about future rate movement. That said, you can weigh some concrete facts into your decision:


- **Rates remain near their highest level in nearly three years** , even after Thursday's decline, with the 30-year fixed at 7.54% and the jumbo and ARM averages at the top of their 52-week ranges.
- **One good day doesn't make a trend.** Thursday's drop was the first meaningful improvement in weeks, and the market's muted reaction to today's jobs report shows how quickly early gains can fade.
- **A rate lock protects you from increases** between now and closing, typically for a set window (often 30–60 days), but it also means you won't benefit if rates drop further after you lock. Many lenders offer float-down options that allow you to lock a rate and then move to a lower rate should it drop materially before closing.


If you already have a mortgage at a higher rate than today's averages, it may be worth checking[when it makes sense to refinance](https://better.com/content/when-to-refinance-mortgage) , which walks through the break-even math against current[refinance rates](https://better.com/refinance-rates) .


Timing a rate lock is ultimately a personal risk decision: how much certainty you want versus how much upside you're willing to give up.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### I have a 620 credit score. Can I still qualify for a mortgage at today's rates, or will I get a much higher rate?


620 is the[minimum qualifying score](https://better.com/content/minimum-credit-score-for-mortgage) for many types of conventional mortgages, but meeting that benchmark won't guarantee mortgage approval. Underwriters also look at your income, debts, down payment size, property type, and other factors to decide whether to approve your loan.


### Is it worth refinancing right now if my current rate is below 7.5%?


For most borrowers, probably not, since today's 30-year fixed average is 7.54%. Refinancing can still make sense in specific situations, such as removing mortgage insurance or changing your loan term, but always do your own math to compare your eventual savings from the new loan to the upfront cost of getting it.


### What's the difference between the rate I see online and the rate a lender will actually offer me?


Published national averages, like the ones on this page, reflect a broad mix of credit scores, down payments, and loan types. Your actual quote is based on your specific credit score, debt-to-income ratio, down payment, property type, and loan amount, so it can land above or below the published average.


### I'm a veteran with no down payment saved. How does a VA loan rate compare to a conventional loan today?


VA loans are currently averaging 7.17%, below the 7.54% conventional 30-year fixed rate, and VA loans don't require a down payment or ongoing mortgage insurance, which conventional loans typically do below 20% down. For eligible veterans and service members, that combination often makes VA loans the lower-cost option overall, not just on rate.


### What happens if I lock my rate today and rates drop before closing?


If you lock your rate, you're generally protected from increases, but you also won't automatically benefit if rates fall further, unless your lender specifically offers a float-down option that lets you capture a lower rate for a fee or under certain conditions. It's worth asking your lender directly whether float-down is available before you lock.


### How does the monthly jobs report affect mortgage rates?


The jobs report is one of the most closely watched economic releases because it shapes expectations for inflation and Fed policy. Weaker-than-expected job growth tends to push mortgage rates lower, while stronger numbers tend to push them higher. Markets also weigh details like the unemployment rate and wage growth, so the reaction doesn't always match the headline job count.


## The bottom line


The 30-year fixed average fell to 7.54% on Thursday, a modest break after reaching 7.60% on Wednesday, its highest level in nearly three years.
